claims.text: In situ cryogenic cooling during HEA additive manufacturing will reduce the thermal gradients and rapid thermal cycling associated with laser powder bed fusion.
In situ cryogenic cooling will produce a more stable melt pool.
In situ cryogenic cooling will refine the HEA microstructure.
In situ cryogenic cooling will reduce fabrication-induced defects in AM HEAs.
In situ cryogenic cooling will improve the dimensional precision of AM HEA components relative to ambient-temperature processing.
In situ cryogenic cooling will improve the mechanical integrity of AM HEA components relative to ambient-temperature processing.
As-built AM HEA components can exhibit porosity, dimensional inaccuracy, residual stress, and non-uniform microstructure due to rapid solidification.
Laser-based HEA additive processing involves rapid heating and cooling with short periods above the melting point.
The intervention should be applied concurrently with layer-by-layer deposition.
A moderated thermal gradient will make melt-pool solidification more uniform and produce a finer grain structure.
A moderated thermal gradient will lower residual stress levels.
Cryogenic cooling reduces localized overheating and steep thermal gradients during laser exposure.
Reduced overheating and thermal gradients diminish melt-pool instabilities and shorten the time available for porosity and microcrack formation.
Reduced melt-pool instability leads to improved dimensional accuracy and more coherent metallurgical bonding.
More coherent metallurgical bonding enhances overall mechanical integrity.
Cryogenically cooled components will have higher tensile strength and ductility than conventionally manufactured controls.
Deep cryogenic post-treatment has increased tensile strength and elongation in laser-deposited Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr HEA.
Ambient-temperature AM using optimized laser parameters still produces notable internal defects and dimensional imprecision.
The benefit may vary with cooling rate, component geometry, and control of other process parameters.
The magnitude of improvement depends on alloy composition and the implementation of cryogenic cooling.
